findings.quote: meet two components whose resistance changes
findings.what: The very first message uses 'components' and 'resistance' before either has been explained. 'Component' is never defined anywhere in the lesson.

findings.quote: First, three quick questions from the last lesson, on current and resistance. What is electric current?
findings.what: The lesson opens with a recall test on another lesson. A first-time learner has not been told any of this here, so her first three experiences are likely to be guessing or getting it wrong.

findings.quote: The push that drives the charge is the potential difference.
findings.what: 'Potential difference' is used here and all through the lesson (1.1b, 1.5c, 2.5, 4.x) but this lesson never explains it.

findings.quote: Which button is about the charge flowing?
findings.what: The hint does not separate the options: all three buttons mention charge, and two mention it flowing.

findings.quote: Second: for the same potential difference, what does a bigger resistance do to the current?
findings.what: The question depends on 'resistance' and 'potential difference' before either is explained. Resistance is only explained on the wrong and don't-know branches, and a girl who answers correctly never gets it.

findings.turn: 1.1b (wrong: It does not change the current)
findings.quote: Not quite: a bigger resistance makes the current smaller, and a smaller resistance makes it bigger. Resistance is how hard it is for charge to flow.
findings.what: This is word for word the reply to 'It makes the current bigger'. It does not address her idea that the current is fixed whatever is in the circuit.

findings.quote: Third: why does a filament lamp's I-V graph curve?

findings.quote: so the current goes up less and less

findings.quote: use the correct symbol for every part, draw the wires as straight lines, and leave no gap where two wires should join
findings.what: Three drawing rules are given in one message.

findings.what: The message immediately before lists all three options: two as rules, and the gap as the thing to avoid. She only has to read back one line.

findings.what: There is no word of care about hot water. The whole method (set up, measure, record, change, repeat) is in one bubble.

findings.what: The message just before the card (4.8a) has already stated R = V ÷ I, and 4.10 and 4.11 say it again.

findings.quote: A component has a potential difference of 30 V across it and a current of 1 A through it. What is its resistance, in ohms (Ω)?
findings.what: Dividing by 1 tests nothing. She gets 30 by copying the number, or by wrongly multiplying, so a right answer shows no understanding. The numbers should be like the worked examples.

findings.quote: Not quite. Check your working and have one more go
findings.what: After a wrong answer she gets the same question with no hint at all, not an easier step.

findings.quote: Then plot a graph: the temperature (or the light intensity) along the bottom, and the resistance up the side.
findings.what: 'Then' follows a practice calculation, and the practical it continues from was several messages back. She will not know what it comes after.

findings.quote: Then plot a graph: the temperature (or the light intensity) along the bottom, and the resistance up the side.
findings.what: The key point says both graphs are downward curves and what that means. The script leaves this out, so key point 4 ends without all of it taught.

findings.quote: Not quite: the water lets you set the thermistor's temperature and measure the temperature with a thermometer.
findings.what: The reply to 'To stop the current' does not say why that idea is wrong. The question also comes after the own-words summary when it belongs straight after 4.6.

findings.quote: Not quite. A battery is two or more cells side by side. That is a lamp.
findings.what: 'That' reads as pointing at the battery description just before it, so it seems to say two cells side by side is a lamp. It should say 'A circle with a cross in it is a lamp'.

findings.quote: Not quite. A battery is two or more cells side by side. That is a resistor.
findings.what: The same dangling 'That': it seems to call the battery a resistor.

findings.quote: Not quite. A fuse is a rectangle with a line through it. That is a variable resistor.
findings.what: 'That' seems to refer to the fuse symbol just described, so it reads as if a rectangle with a line through it is a variable resistor.

findings.quote: Not quite. A fuse is a rectangle with a line through it. That is a lamp.
findings.what: The same dangling 'That': it reads as if the fuse symbol is a lamp.

findings.quote: As the light gets brighter, an LDR's resistance decreases. Brighter light means a lower resistance.
findings.what: The reply says the same thing twice and gives no help with why she might have had it backwards. The 5.4 'It decreases' reply does the same.

findings.quote: A potential difference of 1.2 V is put across a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current through it, in amperes (A)?
findings.what: She has only been shown and practised finding R. Rearranging for current (I = V ÷ R) was never taught or tried in this lesson, so this is not 'the same kind as the worked example'.

overall: No, not as it is. The physics is mostly sound and the thermistor and LDR sections are reasonably paced, but the lesson opens with three recall questions on a lesson she has not had, and uses potential difference, series, parallel and I-V graph before explaining them. Key point 1 describes symbols in words with no picture until seven are done, and teaches series and parallel without ever showing a branched circuit. Before she uses it I would fix those, along with the 4.3 question that needs an untaught fact, the trivial 30 ÷ 1 practice, the quiz question that needs an untaught rearrangement, and the quiz replies where 'That is a lamp' follows the battery or fuse description.
